issues.legal_issue: A second appeal may be entertained only when it involves a substantial question of law, and a new, non-jurisdictional ground unsupported by the pleadings or evidence below cannot be used to overturn concurrent factual findings.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court concurrently found that the land had been permissively occupied for a limited period and rejected the asserted oral sale agreement.
The respondent had not pleaded or argued below that the licence was irrevocable, and no issue or evidence on that ground was presented in the subordinate courts.
The High Court entertained the new ground in second appeal without formulating a substantial question of law and set aside the concurrent findings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in entertaining the new ground or disturbing the concurrent findings in the absence of a formulated substantial question of law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 CPC, as amended in 1976, confines second appeals to cases involving a substantial question of law, which must be stated in the memorandum and formulated by the High Court; another substantial question may be heard only with reasons recorded. A party generally cannot set up a new, non-jurisdictional case in second appeal when it is unsupported by the pleadings or evidence. The Court relied on Chevalier I.I. Iyyappan v. The Dharmodayam Co., which disallowed raising a licence-irrevocability plea for the first time at the appellate stage.

rule.if: second_appeal and nonjurisdictional_new_ground and ground_unsupported_below and no_substantial_question_formulated

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal to a High Court from an appellate decree of a subordinate court.
predicates.nonjurisdictional_new_ground: A party raises a ground that was not part of its case below and that does not concern jurisdiction.
predicates.ground_unsupported_below: The ground is unsupported by the pleadings or evidence presented in the subordinate courts.
predicates.no_substantial_question_formulated: The High Court has not formulated a substantial question of law for deciding the appeal.

issues.definition: When a party raises an unsupported, non-jurisdictional new ground in a second appeal and no substantial question of law has been formulated, the High Court must not entertain that ground.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot make a statutory protection operative in a jurisdiction to which the legislature has not extended the statute, although analogous equitable principles may be considered independently where appropriate.
material_facts: The Easements Act did not apply in Assam.
The High Court nevertheless treated Section 60(b) of that Act as protecting the respondent against eviction, relying on principles of justice, equity and good conscience.
The respondent had denied being a licensee and had asserted that he occupied the land as a purchaser under an oral agreement; the courts had found that sale-agreement account false.
The respondent relied on a later commissioner's report about the structure, although the relevant question concerned the structure raised during the period of permissive use.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not apply Section 60(b) in a jurisdiction where the Act did not apply; the provision could not be made operative by judicial order.
issues.legal_principle: Section 60(b) of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, provides for irrevocability of a licence where the licensee, acting upon it, executes work of a permanent character and incurs expenses. The Court held that a statute not extended to a jurisdiction cannot be applied there by judicial order. The principles of justice, equity and good conscience underlying that provision may independently apply in an appropriate case. The Court distinguished Jagat Singh v. District Board, which applied those principles where a licensee had, acting on the licence and at considerable cost, made permanent works; it also discussed Mathuri v. Bhola Nath, on which Jagat Singh had relied.

predicates.statutory_protection_claimed: A party seeks a benefit under a statutory provision.
predicates.statute_not_applicable_in_jurisdiction: The legislature has not extended the statute to the jurisdiction where the dispute is being heard.
predicates.court_treats_statutory_provision_as_oper: A court proposes to give the statutory provision effect in the dispute despite its non-application there.

issues.definition: If a party claims statutory protection under a statute that does not apply in the jurisdiction, a court must not treat that provision as operative there.

issues.legal_issue: A person whose claim for equitable protection rests on a false account and who does not approach the court with clean hands is not entitled to relief under principles of justice, equity and good conscience.
material_facts: The respondent denied that he was a licensee or had received permission to occupy the land and raise temporary structures.
He claimed instead that he occupied the land as a prospective purchaser under an oral sale agreement.
The courts found the oral sale agreement account false, and the respondent's challenge to the dismissal of his specific-performance suit was unsuccessful.
The respondent sought equitable protection against eviction on the basis of the alleged permanent construction.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming that analogous equitable principles could apply, the respondent was not entitled to relief because his claim rested on a false account and he did not come to court with clean hands.
issues.legal_principle: A court applying equity must promote honesty and good faith and prevent legal fraud; a party seeking equitable relief must come to court with clean hands. The Court considered the equitable principles associated with Section 60(b) of the Easements Act and distinguished Jagat Singh v. District Board, where the licensee had acted on the licence and made permanent works at considerable cost, unlike the respondent's position and conduct.

predicates.equitable_relief_sought: A party asks a court to grant relief on equitable grounds.
predicates.claimant_denied_permission_and_claimed_p: The party denied receiving permission to occupy the property and claimed instead to occupy it under a purchase agreement.
predicates.purchase_claim_found_false: The courts found the party's claimed purchase agreement account false.

issues.definition: A party seeking equitable relief is not entitled to it when the party denied permission and relied instead on a purchase claim that the courts found false.
